This is an interesting post on several counts. First of all it is full of pictures of colourful birds, which I’m sure will be interesting to the kittens up on the PPP ranch. Secondly, the last section of the post is a musing on how you form a ranking and what it means for a ranking to be “fair”. He’s more focused on mathematical/algorithmic rankings than is possible on the T25U25, but the essay feels congruent to some of Cathy’s thoughts on what is interesting about making a ranking.

I am overwhelmed. That entire post is about so much, more I almost think, than the author knows.


I skimmed the math I don’t understand because there is much in there. All models model the modeler. And then what is said about LLM output, what is assumed, what is said about human values vs biases and …. I don’t think there is a line there.


The conclusion that you can’t make an intentionally biased model because the math is then ugly is something Micah McCurdy would say, and yet… look out on the world and find the people who make ugly things on purpose.


What we do when we vote, no matter how seriously or frivolously we take things is reveal ourselves. We model ourselves, and we show ourselves.


I want to believe in the world were LLMs are therefore fair because they are the sum of us, but I don’t. Alas, I do not.


Also the bird pictures are outstandingly glorious.


Oh, also the entire bit about lack of sampled plumage is totally me looking at one of those “I tracked 7 games in junior, and now I know this person’s soul.”


Anyhow I need to read that again. There’s a thing I could bang on about about taxation and how they decide who to audit and who to ask for information that gets very directly at the moral implications of the deniability thing. Deniability as innocence is a hell of a concept.


That’s just gorgeous stuff in all ways. The internet is good.

This was a fantastic article that was extremely relevant to my interests. If you’ll allow me to hobby-dump, I hope that you’ll find something interesting in the perspective of someone grappling with questions of fairness in ranking in a rather different field. For my part, your framework clarified something I’ve been thinking about for a year, and so I figured I would share an independent application of it.

For the last year and change, my singular obsession has been ranking players in competitive Super Smash Bros. Melee. It started in August of 2025 with an intuitive hunch that a particular player had been underrated on the community’s official Summer 2025 ranking. This hunch motivated me to apply well-established ranking algorithms to the competitive Melee data from that season. I started with Glicko-2, but quickly transitioned to using a Bradley-Terry model thanks to the suggestion of an insightful commenter.

Several months later, in December, I put out my year-end 2025 rankings in advance of the release of the community’s official SSBMRank (conducted via panel vote). When SSBMRank began rolling out, I was surprised to see another particular player whom I had previously identified as underrated (and thus championed) was again underrated by a considerable margin. I expressed my feelings about the placement, and a common sentiment was that I was systematically overrating European players due to a closed-pool effect.

After further investigation, I attempted to defend my ranking system by demonstrating its accuracy on a suite of tests versus several other ranking systems.

It would be an understatement to say that many people in the competitive Super Smash Bros. Melee community were not fond of my rankings, in large part because of a long-standing skepticism toward algorithmic rankings. Screenshot of an interactive 3D visualization titled 'heads are angles, not slices,' explaining multi-head attention in transformers. A dark-themed web app shows three intertwined helical strands of points (pink, tan, and teal, representing three attention heads) spiraling around a central white helix (the residual stream), with three translucent planes cutting through the structure to represent each head's subspace. Left sidebar controls include sliders for residual stream size, head visibility checkboxes, ray/shadow projection, and angle-between-heads adjustment, plus buttons for 'free,' 'down head 0,' 'down head 1,' and 'down head 2' configurations. Explanatory text describes how each head views the shared residual stream as a projected shadow, and a footnote clarifies that the 3D/2D visualization is a simplified stand-in for a higher-dimensional (160-dim, 32-dim per head) system.

Why we switched from Git to a transactional DB
December 2026
With agents producing so much code, we started to realize that Git was solving the wrong problem for our workflow.
Git is fantastic for humans. Its commit / branch / merge model matches how people think about work: make some changes, save a checkpoint, try something, maybe roll it back, then merge when you're ready. But when dozens of agents are continuously writing, rewriting, and coordinating code, that model starts to get in the way.
Agents don't think in branches. They operate in loops that are short-lived, parallel, and relentless.
They touch the same files, refactor the same functions, and react to each other's changes constantly. In that environment, branches become a coordination tax. Merges become noisy negotiations. And the working tree becomes a shared mutable state that's easy to corrupt.
We switched to a transactional database for our code state.
Every change an agent makes is a transaction. It's atomic, ordered, and recorded with metadata about who (which agent), why, and what was changed. The entire codebase at any point in time is a consistent snapshot you can query. Rollbacks are trivial. Audit trails are built in. And because it's a database, we get concurrency control, constraints, and durability out of the box.
This unlocked a few big things for us: true parallel agent work without stepping on each other, precise semantic diffs, fast queries over history, and the ability to reproduce any past state exactly. It also let us build higher-level workflows-like automated refactoring and large-scale edits-as safe, observable operations instead of risky git gymnastics.
To be clear, we still love Git. It's unmatched for distribution, open-source collaboration, and the broader ecosystem around it. For outward-facing projects, we'll keep using it.
But internally, for an agent-heavy world, we wanted stronger invariants and cleaner coordination.
